Sourced Statements: “It is gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said in a statement.
Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Greenland's leader, said “the agreement recognizes Greenland's interests and our place in international cooperation. This is to the benefit of us all.”

The U.S. will have a permanent military presence on Greenland, even if it becomes an independent nation, allowing for an increase in the number of bases there, a State Department official said. The agreement also bans countries who aren't part of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization—notably China and Russia—from establishing their own base or making investments on the island that threaten U.S. security, the official said.
“Greenland will forever be part of the strategic defense area of North America and exclude any adversary from it and the surrounding area,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.
Allies were incensed when Trump raised the possibility of a military operation against a fellow NATO member to seize the territory.

Denmark had already blocked NATO adversaries from making sensitive business investments in Greenland, especially for rare earths, and was unlikely to allow countries like China and Russia to establish a military base on allied territory, analysts said.

Successive U.S.-Danish agreements, dating back to the early months of Nazi Germany’s occupation of Denmark, have given the American military broad rights to station troops, build bases, operate ports or fly warplanes in Greenland.
